interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: MetaResearcher: Scaling Deep Research via Self-Reflective Reinforcement Learning in Adversarial Virtual Environments
papers.authors: Wei Yu , Suxing Liu , Minjie Yu , Jiahao Wang , Zhijian Zheng , Haocheng Deng , Bing Li
papers.abstract: Deep research agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in autonomous information gathering and synthesis, yet their training remains constrained by the static nature of simulated environments, the limits of fact-retrieval-only task designs, and the inefficiency of outcome-based reinforcement learning. In this work, we propose MetaResearcher, a novel framework that scales deep research agent training across four synergistic dimensions. First, we introduce an Evolving Virtual World that injects temporal dynamics and adversarial misinformation into the training environment, forcing agents to develop source credibility assessment and temporal conflict resolution skills. Second, we design Discovery-Oriented Tasks -- including hypothesis generation and contradiction resolution -- that transcend simple fact retrieval and push agents toward genuine research behaviors. Third, we propose a Self-Reflective Meta-Reward mechanism within the GRPO framework that jointly optimizes for answer correctness, search path efficiency, reflection depth, and tool call diversity, directly addressing the repetitive action loop problem observed in prior work. Fourth, we introduce a Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Swarm architecture comprising specialized Scout, Filter, and Synthesizer models that learn collaborative research strategies through coordinated reinforcement learning. Built upon the LiteResearcher infrastructure, MetaResearcher requires zero marginal API cost for training while targeting substantial improvements in both benchmark performance (GAIA, Xbench-DS) and epistemic robustness under adversarial conditions. We present the complete framework design, training methodology, and planned experimental validation.
papers.Reasons for match: This paper directly addresses deep research agents, self-reflective reinforcement learning, and multi-agent swarms for autonomous information gathering and synthesis, which are highly relevant to automated scientific discovery and LLM agents for literature review and data analysis in astronomy.
papers.Short digest: This paper proposes MetaResearcher, a framework for scaling deep research agent training across four dimensions: an evolving virtual world with adversarial misinformation, discovery-oriented tasks beyond fact retrieval, a self-reflective meta-reward mechanism, and a heterogeneous multi-agent swarm architecture. The core idea is to train agents to develop source credibility assessment, temporal conflict resolution, and collaborative research strategies through reinforcement learning in adversarial environments. This is highly relevant to astronomy because it could enable automated literature review, hypothesis generation, and contradiction resolution across astronomical datasets and publications. For example, an astronomer could use such an agent to synthesize findings from JWST papers on little red dots, identify conflicting results, and propose new observational tests. A key limitation is that the framework is designed for general research tasks and may require significant adaptation to handle domain-specific astronomical data formats, coordinate systems, and instrument characteristics. Before investing time, check whether the agent can ingest astronomical catalogs, spectra, and images, or if it is limited to text-based literature.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for evaluation on GAIA and Xbench-DS benchmarks to see if the agent handles multi-step research tasks. Check whether the Evolving Virtual World includes astronomical data or only general web text. Examine the Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Swarm architecture to see if Scout, Filter, and Synthesizer models can be specialized for astronomy workflows. Look for discussion of tool use (e.g., API calls to databases, code execution) that could be adapted for astronomical data analysis.

papers.title: Language-Instructed Vision Embeddings for Controllable and Generalizable Perception
papers.authors: Chengzhi Mao , Xudong Lin , Wen-Sheng Chu
papers.abstract: Vision foundation models are typically trained as static feature extractors, placing the burden of task adaptation onto large downstream models. We propose an alternative paradigm: instead of solely feeding visual features into language models, we use language itself to dynamically guide the vision encoder. Our method, Language-Instructed Vision Embeddings (LIVE), leverages language as high-level guidance to produce task-centric embeddings at inference time, removing the need for task-specific retraining. This enables the encoder to focus on contextually relevant aspects of the input, yielding more controllable and generalizable representations. Empirically, LIVE reduces visual hallucinations (+34 points on MMVP), surpasses vision-language models with orders of magnitude more parameters on visual question answering, and generalizes to unseen instructions and tasks -- offering a direct path toward adaptive, instruction-driven visual intelligence.
papers.Reasons for match: Paper proposes language-instructed vision embeddings (LIVE) that use language to dynamically guide vision encoders, directly relevant to multimodal models for astronomy (e.g., combining images and text queries for source classification or anomaly detection).
papers.Short digest: This paper addresses the problem that vision foundation models are static feature extractors, requiring large downstream models for task adaptation. It proposes LIVE, which uses language instructions to dynamically guide the vision encoder at inference time, producing task-centric embeddings without retraining. This reduces visual hallucinations and improves generalization to unseen instructions. This matters for astronomy because it could enable a single vision encoder to perform multiple tasks (e.g., morphology classification, anomaly detection, source finding) based on natural language queries from a user. A concrete workflow would be to use LIVE to query JWST images for 'little red dots' or 'high-redshift galaxy candidates' without retraining the encoder. A caveat is that the paper evaluates on general vision tasks (VQA, MMVP) and not on astronomical images; the method's performance on scientific images with different statistics is unknown. Before investing time, check if the method requires paired language-image data for training, which is scarce in astronomy.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for experiments on out-of-distribution images or domains beyond natural images.
Check whether the language guidance is effective for fine-grained visual features (e.g., morphological details) or only for coarse categories.
Verify if the method can be applied to grayscale or multi-band astronomical images without modification.

papers.title: TerraMARS: A Domain-Adapted Small-Language-Model Pipeline for Mars Terraforming Literature
papers.authors: Jyotsna Singh , Ash Black , Jeff Larsen , Scott R. Saleska
papers.abstract: Researchers are interested in learning about Mars so that it may eventually become habitable for humans. To achieve this, there is a need for comprehensive knowledge of the planet's atmosphere, hydrology, surface chemistry, radiation environment, and spatial features through the scientific literature. These contain valuable information and meaningful quantitative constraints that can be used in other models and studies, such as habitability assessment and future terraforming studies. We present TerraMARS, an end-to-end information extraction pipeline that combines a domain-adapted Small Language Model to answer Mars terraforming-related questions and convert unstructured Mars science text into machine-readable structured outputs in JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format. A corpus of open-access papers is collected and processed using a multistage retrieval and chunking framework. Google Gemma 3 1B was adapted to the domain using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) fine-tuning on Mars-specific question-answering and information extraction datasets. The resulting pipeline generates both types of output and provides a foundation for integrating knowledge from scientific literature into downstream applications like digital twins and habitability modeling for Mars. The output from this pipeline looks promising, but further improvements are needed to increase extraction accuracy and factual consistency.
papers.Reasons for match: Domain-adapted small language model for Mars terraforming literature; directly relevant to using LLMs for scientific literature extraction in astronomy.
papers.Short digest: This paper presents TerraMARS, a pipeline that uses a fine-tuned small language model (Gemma 3 1B with QLoRA) to extract structured information from Mars science literature into JSON format. The system uses multistage retrieval and chunking to answer domain-specific questions and convert unstructured text into machine-readable data. For astronomy, this is directly applicable to extracting physical parameters from exoplanet or galaxy literature, building knowledge graphs for high-redshift galaxies, or automating literature reviews for JWST results. The pipeline could be adapted to extract spectroscopic redshifts, emission-line fluxes, or morphological classifications from papers. However, the current domain is Mars terraforming, not astronomy, and the extraction accuracy needs improvement. The use of QLoRA for domain adaptation is a practical approach that could be replicated with astronomy-specific datasets.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the accuracy of information extraction on Mars-specific questions and whether the pipeline handles numerical constraints (e.g., temperature ranges).
Look for details on the chunking and retrieval strategy, which would need adaptation for astronomy papers with complex figures and tables.
Examine the QLoRA fine-tuning recipe to assess feasibility of retraining on astronomy literature.

papers.title: Prompt, Plan, Extract: Zero-Shot Agentic LLMs Workflows for Lung Pathology Extraction from Clinical Narratives
papers.authors: Aman Pathak (1), Cheng Peng (1), Mengxian Lyu (1), Ziyi Chen (1), Reema Solan (1), Sankalp Talankar (1), Yasir Khan (1), Hiren Mehta (2), Aokun Chen (3), Yi Guo (1), Yonghui Wu (1)
papers.abstract: Information extraction from pathology reports is essential for cancer staging, tumor registry population. Yet key data remains embedded in narrative reports, making manual extraction labor-intensive and error-prone. Traditional supervised Natural Language Processing pipelines address this through fully supervised Named Entity Recognition and Relation Extraction, but require expensive manual annotation and suffer cascading failures when upstream entities are missed. In this study, we developed a zero-shot, agentic workflow, and evaluated five open-source generative Large Language Models (LLMs) to populate 13 College of American Pathologists synoptic fields from lung resection pathology reports. We compared them against a state-of-the-art supervised GatorTron NER-RE baseline using a novel, registry-aligned evaluation framework. The baseline achieved Micro-F1of 0.960, while the best zero-shot model (GPT-OSS-20B) achieved Micro-F1 of 0.893 (recall: 0.949), accurately extracting complex relations like Pathologic Stage without task-specific training. These results suggest that open-source, zero-shot agentic LLMs are a low-cost solution for extracting lung pathology information.
papers.Reasons for match: Paper directly demonstrates a zero-shot LLM agent for structured information extraction from clinical narratives, a workflow directly transferable to extracting astronomical parameters from paper text or telescope logs.
papers.Short digest: This paper addresses the problem of extracting structured data (e.g., cancer stage) from unstructured pathology reports without any training data. It develops a zero-shot agentic workflow using open-source LLMs to populate 13 synoptic fields, achieving high recall (0.949) compared to a supervised baseline. For astronomy, this is directly relevant: an agent could extract redshifts, AGN fractions, or morphological classifications from JWST paper PDFs or observing proposals. A concrete workflow would be an agent that reads a set of papers on little red dots and populates a table with their redshifts, masses, and AGN indicators. The main caveat is that the paper uses a specific medical ontology (CAP synoptic fields), and the agent's prompts and workflow would need to be redesigned for astronomical ontologies and the more varied writing styles in astronomy papers.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the prompt structure: does the agent use chain-of-thought or tool calling? This will inform how to design prompts for astronomical extraction.
Look for the evaluation framework: how do they handle partial matches or missing fields? This is crucial for noisy astronomical literature.

papers.title: A Systematic Evaluation of Black-Box Uncertainty Estimation Methods for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across a wide range of tasks, their outputs often remain unreliable and may contain hallucinations, making uncertainty estimation (UE) essential for building trustworthy LLMs. In practice, many mainstream LLMs are only accessible through restricted APIs, where internal signals such as logits and hidden states are unavailable, making black-box UE especially important. However, existing work on black-box UE for LLMs remains fragmented in methodology and lacks a unified empirical comparison. To address this gap, we present a systematic review of black-box UE methods and organize them into five categories: verbalization-based, sampling-based, explanation-based, multi-agent, and hybrid methods. We further build a unified evaluation framework and benchmark 24 representative methods across 4 models and 4 dataset settings. Our results show that no single method consistently dominates across all settings. Nevertheless, methods that reason over and compare candidates in the answer space are generally effective, and hybrid methods that combine multiple uncertainty signals perform well under most conditions. By releasing the benchmark data and a unified evaluation framework, we aim to facilitate reproducible comparisons and support future research, while our empirical findings provide practical guidance for developing future black-box UE methods for LLMs.
papers.Reasons for match: Paper provides a systematic evaluation of black-box uncertainty estimation methods for LLMs, which is directly relevant for building trustworthy AI agents for astronomy.
papers.Short digest: This paper addresses the problem of estimating uncertainty in LLM outputs when only the API is accessible (no logits or hidden states). It systematically reviews and benchmarks 24 black-box UE methods across 4 models and 4 datasets, finding that no single method dominates but hybrid methods combining multiple signals perform well. For astronomy, this is crucial for building reliable research agents that can flag uncertain classifications or literature extractions. A concrete workflow would be using a black-box UE method to assess the confidence of an LLM agent's answer when asked 'Is this galaxy an AGN?' based on a paper abstract. The main caveat is that the benchmark uses general NLP tasks (e.g., question answering, summarization), and the performance of these UE methods on domain-specific astronomical tasks (e.g., extracting redshifts from text) is unknown.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the list of UE methods: are any of them practical for a research agent (e.g., sampling-based or verbalization-based) without requiring multiple API calls?
Look for the evaluation on 'explanation-based' methods: do they provide calibrated uncertainty or just verbose justifications?

papers.title: Multi-Agent Transactive Memory
papers.authors: To Eun Kim , Xuhong He , Dishank Jain , Ambuj Agrawal , Negar Arabzadeh , Fernando Diaz
papers.subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Computation and Language (cs.CL); Information Retrieval (cs.IR)
papers.abstract: The decentralized deployment of LLM agents with diverse capabilities across diverse tasks motivates infrastructure for knowledge sharing across heterogeneous agent populations. Just as search engines index human-generated artifacts to support human problem solving, retrieval systems can organize agent-generated artifacts for reuse across agent populations. We extend retrieval-augmented generation - which demonstrates the value of human-authored artifacts to individual agents - to retrieval of agent-generated artifacts supporting a population of agents. In particular, agent trajectories encode reusable procedural knowledge, yet these artifacts are typically discarded after a single use or retained only by the producing agent, forcing newly instantiated agents to repeatedly rediscover existing solutions. We propose Multi-Agent Transactive Memory (MATM), a framework for population-level storage and retrieval of agent-generated trajectories, where producer agents contribute trajectories to a shared repository and consumer agents retrieve them to improve task execution. We focus on interactive environments (ALFWorld and WebArena), where trajectories are long and encode especially rich procedural structure. Our experiments demonstrate that retrieving trajectories from MATM improves downstream task performance and reduces interaction steps without coordination or joint training. These results position MATM as a design pattern for population-level experience sharing in open agent ecosystems.
papers.Reasons for match: This paper proposes a multi-agent transactive memory framework for storing and retrieving agent trajectories, which is highly relevant to LLM agents for scientific workflows and reproducible research. The idea of sharing procedural knowledge across agents could accelerate astronomical data analysis pipelines.
papers.Short digest: This paper proposes Multi-Agent Transactive Memory (MATM), a framework for population-level storage and retrieval of LLM agent trajectories, where producer agents contribute trajectories to a shared repository and consumer agents retrieve them to improve task execution. The key idea is to extend retrieval-augmented generation to agent-generated artifacts, enabling reuse of procedural knowledge across heterogeneous agent populations. This is highly relevant to astronomy because it could enable a community of AI agents to share successful analysis workflows for JWST data, such as SED fitting or source classification. For example, an agent that successfully deblends a crowded field could store its trajectory for other agents to reuse. A limitation is that the framework is evaluated on interactive environments (ALFWorld, WebArena) and may need adaptation for astronomical data analysis tools. Before investing time, check if the trajectory representation can capture the complex dependencies of astronomical data pipelines (e.g., calibration, stacking, fitting).
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for the trajectory representation and how procedural knowledge is encoded. Check the retrieval mechanism and whether it supports semantic search over trajectories. Examine the downstream task performance improvement and reduction in interaction steps. Look for discussion of scalability to large agent populations and whether the framework handles heterogeneous agent capabilities.

papers.title: ScaffoldAgent: Utility-Guided Dynamic Outline Optimization for Open-Ended Deep Research
papers.authors: Zhibang Yang , Xinke Jiang , Yuzhen Xiao , Ruizhe Zhang , Yue Fang , XinFei Wan , Zhengxing Song , Yuxuan Liu , Yuheng Huang , Xu Chu , Junfeng Zhao , Yasha Wang
papers.abstract: Open-ended deep research (OEDR) requires systems to acquire knowledge through multi-round retrieval and generate coherent long-form reports. The outline plays a central role as a structural scaffold that coordinates retrieval, evidence organization, and generation. However, existing methods either fix the outline before writing or refine it with local heuristics, leading to scaffold drift under continuous information accumulation and delayed feedback for evaluating outline modifications. We propose ScaffoldAgent, a utility-guided dynamic outline optimization framework for OEDR. ScaffoldAgent models outline evolution as a structured decision process with three operations: Expansion, Contraction, and Revision, enabling controlled updates to the report scaffold. It further introduces a utility-guided feedback mechanism that estimates the downstream value of each outline operation from retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality. The resulting utility signal guides node selection, operation scheduling, and termination during inference. Experiments on DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearch Gym show that ScaffoldAgent consistently improves long-form report generation and factual grounding over existing deep research agents.
papers.Reasons for match: This paper directly addresses open-ended deep research with LLM agents, which is highly relevant to automated scientific discovery and literature review workflows in astronomy.
papers.Short digest: The paper tackles the problem of generating coherent long-form research reports through multi-round retrieval, where a static outline can drift as information accumulates. The main idea is ScaffoldAgent, a framework that treats outline evolution as a structured decision process with three operations—Expansion, Contraction, and Revision—and uses a utility-guided feedback mechanism to evaluate each operation's downstream value. For astronomy, this could automate literature review and synthesis tasks, such as generating a report on recent JWST high-redshift galaxy findings. I could imagine using it to produce a structured summary of papers on little red dots or AGN from a set of retrieved abstracts. A key caveat is that the method is designed for text-based research and may need adaptation to handle domain-specific terminology or multimodal inputs like spectra and images.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the utility-guided feedback mechanism incorporates domain-specific metrics (e.g., citation relevance or factual accuracy for astronomy).
Look for evaluation on scientific or technical domains beyond general web-based research.
Examine the outline operations (Expansion, Contraction, Revision) for any constraints on handling hierarchical or multi-modal outlines.

papers.title: SARLO-80: Worldwide Slant SAR Language Optic Dataset 80cm
papers.authors: Solène Debuysère , Nicolas Trouvé , Nathan Letheule , Elise Colin , Georgia Channing
papers.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Databases (cs.DB)
papers.abstract: Multimodal foundation models have advanced rapidly thanks to large optical benchmarks, but comparable resources for synthetic aperture radar (SAR) remain limited. Existing SAR--optical datasets largely rely on low-resolution, intensity-only Ground Range Detected~(GRD) products and do not preserve complex-valued SAR measurements or native acquisition geometry, which restricts physically grounded multimodal learning. In particular, large-scale public datasets combining very-high-resolution (VHR) SAR SLC, aligned optical imagery, and natural-language descriptions are still lacking. We present a VHR SAR--optical--text dataset built from open-access Umbra spotlight acquisitions distributed as Sensor Independent Complex Data (SICD). From around 2,500 worldwide scenes (VV/HH, 20cm--2m native resolution), we standardize all SAR data to an 80cm slant-range grid via band-limited FFT resampling and tile the imagery into 1024 by 1024 patches. For each SAR patch, we retrieve a high-resolution optical tile and warp it into the SAR grid using local coordinate correspondences for local pixel-level alignment. We further generate three caption variants (SHORT/MID/LONG) per sample to support vision--language training and evaluation. Our dataset contains 119,566 triplets (complex and amplitude slant-range SAR patch, aligned optical patch, natural-language description) covering 257 locations across 72 countries and a broad range of land types and infrastructures. We release fixed train/validation/test splits and the full preprocessing and baseline code to enable reproducible benchmarks for multimodal alignment on cross-modal retrieval and conditional generation in native SAR geometry. The dataset is publicly available on the Hugging Face Hub at this https URL .
